howItWorks.title: How Progressive Muscle Relaxation Works
howItWorks.description1: Progressive muscle relaxation means tensing and then releasing different muscle groups, one after another. The contrast between tension and release helps you feel relaxation and recognise it better.
howItWorks.description2: Anxiety often comes with tension we are not aware of: raised shoulders, a clenched jaw… As each area lets go, many people feel their body relax and their breathing slow down.
howItWorks.description3: With regular practice, you notice tension building earlier and learn to release it before it accumulates.

tensionContrast.title: Contrast
tensionContrast.description: Tensing first makes the release easier to feel.

nervousSystemShift.title: Body relaxation
nervousSystemShift.description: Releasing the muscles often comes with calmer breathing and a sense of ease.

bodyAwareness.title: Listening to your body
bodyAwareness.description: Practice helps you spot tension during the day and let it go.

science.title: What Studies Say
science.description: Progressive muscle relaxation is one of the oldest and most studied relaxation techniques. Syntheses of studies show a medium effect on anxiety.
science.bottomLine: progressive muscle relaxation is a safe technique that helps many people release tension and feel calmer. The effect is clearer with regular practice.

meta.title: What many studies show
meta.who: About 1,000 adults: students, volunteers, patients with a medical illness or a psychological disorder.
meta.what: Researchers pooled 10 years of studies on relaxation techniques, progressive muscle relaxation being the most studied.
meta.result: Relaxation clearly reduced anxiety (medium effect). Longer programmes and home practice gave better results.
meta.caution: An older synthesis (2008), with studies of uneven quality.

hospital.title: In hospitalised patients
hospital.who: 51 adults hospitalised with COVID-19, in China.
hospital.what: 20 to 30 minutes of progressive muscle relaxation with deep breathing, every day for 5 days, compared with usual care.
hospital.result: After 5 days, anxiety had decreased and sleep had improved in the relaxation group, but not in the other group.
hospital.caution: Small group, short duration, unclear method for allocating patients.

students.title: In nursing students
students.who: 90 first-year nursing students before their first placement, in Palestine.
students.what: 5 group sessions of 45 minutes, plus 10 to 15 minutes of daily practice at home.
students.result: Students' anxiety had clearly decreased when they started their placement.
students.caution: Without a comparison group, we cannot tell how much of the improvement is due to relaxation.

whenToPractice.title: When to Practice
items: When you feel physical tension building in your body—tight shoulders, clenched jaw, or muscle stiffness
Before stressful events like presentations, exams, or medical appointments to release anticipatory tension
At the end of your workday to release accumulated physical stress and transition into relaxation
Before bed to release physical tension that might interfere with falling asleep or staying asleep

whatYoullNotice.title: What You Might Notice
items: Tension you had not been aware of
Relaxation spreading through your body as each area lets go
With practice, an easier time releasing tension during the day

position.title: Position
position.description: Lie down or recline in a comfortable chair where your entire body can be supported. Remove tight clothing and ensure you won't be interrupted for 12-15 minutes.

technique.title: Technique
technique.description: Tense each muscle group firmly but not to the point of pain or cramping. Hold for 10 seconds, then release completely and notice the contrast for another 10 seconds before moving on.

focus.title: Focus
focus.description: Pay attention to the difference between tension and relaxation in each muscle group. This awareness is key to recognizing and releasing tension in daily life.
